tone_statements.citation: Chaperon, Brandon. 2026. A negative alternation: Negation head movement allomorphy in Igala. In Vicki Carstens, Katherine Russell, Olawale Akingbade, Deborah Morton & Michael Diercks (eds.), Pamoja tena 'Together again': African linguistics after COVID (Contemporary African Linguistics), 43-62. Berlin: Language Science Press.
tone_statements.quote: Pre-verbal negation surfaces as extra-high tone on the subject in finite clauses similar to some dialects of Igbo (Emenanjo 1985, Ndimele 1995, Obiamalu 2013) and the Benue–Congo languages Efik (Mensah 2001) and Ibibio (Essien 1990), where negation can be marked by tone only, as in (1). [...] Tonal negation occurs in declaratives, polar interrogatives, and imperatives [...]. This form expones an extra-high tone on the last vowel of the subject, which always precedes the verb [...]. [p. 55:] Subject clitics typically surface with a low tone; when they surface with a mid tone, an optative reading arises, as in (25).
tone_statements.locator: p. 43 (section 1 Introduction), p. 45 (section 2.1 Tonal negation), p. 55 (section 4.1.2 Modals)

tone_statements.citation: Omachonu, Gideon Sunday & Williams Sunday Onogu. 2012. Determining Compoundhood in Ígálà: From Universal to Language Specific Focus. Journal of Universal Language 13(2): 91-117.
tone_statements.quote: For all Ígálà data used in this paper, tone is marked as follows: v́ for High, v̀ for Low but Mid tone is left unmarked. [...] Besides, it appears the nominalising affixes in (2a-c) (prefixes ù, á, é) have their own inherent tones as they neither go on tone copying nor polarization but the tones are either high or low as nouns in Ígálà do not begin on mid tone.

sources.citation: Adeniyi, Kolawole. 2017. The limits of perception in the tonal orthographies of three-tone systems. Linguistik Online 84(5), section 2.3 'Igala' (pp. 10-11). DOI 10.13092/lo.84.3844
sources.note: Gives Igala's 28 consonants and 7 vowels (after Ejeba 2009) and states 'Igala contrasts three tone heights, H, M, and L', with contour tones derived by assimilation (falling L after H, rising H after L, citing Akinkugbe 1978). The word 'stress' does not occur in the article.

sources.citation: Fresco, Edward M. 1969. The tones of the Yoruba and Igala disyllabic noun prefix. Journal of West African Languages 6(1): 31-34
sources.note: Scan scanned (no text). Compares tone combinations on VCV nouns in Igala and Yoruba (e.g. Igala una 'fire', oma 'child'); no mention of stress, accent or prominence anywhere in the four pages.

sources.citation: Ejeba, Salem Ochala. 2023. Igala concord system. Journal of West African Languages 50 (Golden Jubilee edition): 85-103
sources.note: Morphosyntax paper. Only note on prosody: high tone marked with acute, low with grave, mid unmarked; subject clitics are tonally underspecified. No mention of stress.

sources.citation: Momoh, Mahmud. 2023. Vowels and the Igala language resources. Proceedings of the Fourth Workshop on Resources for African Indigenous Languages (RAIL 2023), ACL. DOI 10.18653/v1/2023.rail-1.12
sources.note: Non-linguist lexicographic note; calls Igala 'a tone-based language' and proposes an ad-hoc diacritic system (five 'tones', long vowels 'stressed with falling tones'); no rule for word stress and not a reliable phonological description.

sources.note: Formal-syntax chapter whose core data are grammatical tone: standard (pre-verbal) negation is exponed by an extra-high tone docking on the last vowel of the subject ('tonal negation') in declaratives, polar questions, imperatives and finite embedded clauses, alternating with the particle ma̋ under A'-movement/nominalisation; a conditional is likewise marked by an extra-high tone on the subject, and subject clitics, normally low-toned, take mid tone for the optative. Transcription distinguishes low (grave), mid (macron), high (acute), extra-high (double acute) and rising/falling marks. No stat…

sources.citation: Omachonu, Gideon Sunday & Williams Sunday Onogu. 2012. Determining Compoundhood in Ígálà: From Universal to Language Specific Focus. Journal of Universal Language 13(2): 91-117.
sources.quote: For all Ígálà data used in this paper, tone is marked as follows: v́ for High, v̀ for Low but Mid tone is left unmarked. [...] Besides, it appears the nominalising affixes in (2a-c) (prefixes ù, á, é) have their own inherent tones as they neither go on tone copying nor polarization but the tones are either high or low as nouns in Ígálà do not begin on mid tone.
sources.note: Morphology paper (compounding) with first-hand tone conventions and remarks: data are tone-marked with acute = High, grave = Low, Mid unmarked (three level tones); nominalising prefixes ù-, á-, é- carry inherent H or L tone, and nouns in Ígálà never begin on a Mid tone; tonal behaviour does not distinguish nominal compounds from phrases because compounds keep the tonal patterns of their phrasal counterparts (unlike e.g. Krio H-deletion/L-spreading).
